message:
test(observe): pin the endpoint rule across all three runtimes

Three implementations of one rule, and they were wrong together. Every
client derived the observe port as the http port plus one, so behind TLS on
443 they all sent the probe to 444. Nothing answers there: the host never
completed a heartbeat and never appeared in a list, the viewer never reached
/api/connect and so never learned the relay address. Every suite passed the
entire time, because every suite had made the same assumption as the code it
was testing.

That is what a shared vector file is for, and there was already one for
version comparison. apps/shared/observe_endpoint_vectors.txt states the rule
in prose and then in rows: where the port is read from, what is not a port,
what an advertisement outranks, why https has no default and 444 is not one,
and what happens to an advertised host the server never validated.

The C++ and Kotlin suites read it and must answer identically. Both also
assert they read a minimum number of rows -- a shared-vector test's own
failure mode is passing green over a file it stopped finding.

The JS leg is different on purpose. The server does not parse this, it
emits it, so checking that it agrees with the clients means checking the
document it produces is one of the shapes those rules accept. It starts its
own servers and holds the real responses against the rules: the
advertisement is nested where the clients look and not at the top level,
the port is a whole number in range, /healthz and login and register all
carry the same value, and a port the server cannot honour is left out
entirely rather than published as something the vectors say is not a port.
Both clients would discard such a value -- but a server that emitted it
would be relying on that, and one of them dialling 0 is the failure this
exists to prevent.
